title: How do you prepare AML/CTF training evidence for an AUSTRAC compliance assessment?
description: What AUSTRAC expects to see for AML/CTF personnel training under the reformed Act and 2025 Rules, the records that show it, and a preparation checklist.
shortAnswer: To prepare AML/CTF training evidence for an Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC) compliance assessment, show that your policies provide initial and ongoing training tailored to each person's functions and risks, that a register records completions and due dates, that you test understanding and act on gaps, and that training content matches your current program. AUSTRAC guidance lists the records that demonstrate this, and its 2026 to 2027 priorities target programs that are not applied in daily operations.
keyTakeaways: The training obligation sits in section 26F(4)(e) of the AML/CTF Act and section 5-9 of the AML/CTF Rules 2025: initial and ongoing training, tailored to function, risk, and responsibilities, delivered in a way people understand.
AUSTRAC expects a training plan, a register of completion dates and next due dates, monitoring of effectiveness, and evidence that people retain and apply what they learned.

Records must be reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance (Act section 116); AUSTRAC lists training content, schedules, and a register of attendance, results, completion, and action on non-attendance as examples.

AUSTRAC's priorities for 2026 to 2027 focus interventions on reporting entities whose AML/CTF programs are not applied in daily operations, and on checking that newly regulated businesses have trained staff on their program.
AUSTRAC e-learning modules can support training but cannot be relied on alone, because training must be tailored to the person.

sections.heading: What does AUSTRAC look at when it assesses AML/CTF training?

blocks.text: AUSTRAC looks at whether your AML/CTF policies provide for training and whether that training actually happens, is tailored, and works. Its [AML/CTF training guidance](https://www.austrac.gov.au/industry-and-business/obligations-and-guidance/your-amlctf-program/personnel-due-diligence-and-training/amlctf-training) links the obligation to Act section 26F(4)(e) and Rules section 5-9, and states that AUSTRAC expects reporting entities to do the following and describe how in their policies:

items: develop a training plan and schedule tailored training to different roles and their relevant risks;
include updates on regulatory changes and emerging risks in training material;
take steps to make sure personnel are getting training;
use a register to record completion dates and track when further training is due;
monitor the effectiveness of training; and
evaluate whether personnel retain knowledge and apply it appropriately.

blocks.text: AUSTRAC's [compliance report guidance](https://www.austrac.gov.au/industry-and-business/obligations-and-guidance/your-amlctf-program/reporting-us/annual-compliance-reports) says information in annual compliance reports helps it develop supervision campaigns and assessments. The obligations themselves are explained on the [AUSTRAC AML/CTF training requirements page](/regulations/austrac-aml-ctf-training-requirements).

sections.heading: What is AUSTRAC focusing on in 2026 to 2027?

blocks.text: AUSTRAC is focusing on programs that exist on paper but are not applied in practice, and on whether newly regulated businesses have the basics in place, including trained staff. Reformed obligations for existing reporting entities started on 31 March 2026, and services typically provided by lawyers, accountants, conveyancers, real estate agents, dealers in precious metals and stones, and trust and company service providers were regulated from 1 July 2026.

blocks.title: AUSTRAC regulatory priorities 2026 to 2027
blocks.text: AUSTRAC states it will focus its regulatory interventions on reporting entities in sectors regulated before 31 March "who don't manage their ML/TF risks effectively. This includes those with AML/CTF programs that are not applied in their daily operations."

AUSTRAC's [May 2026 regulator statement of expectations](https://www.austrac.gov.au/news-and-media/article/update-regulator-statement-expectations-may-2026) says it expects newly regulated businesses to be enrolled, have an AML/CTF program and compliance officer, train staff on the program, and be ready to report suspicious matters, and that it expects "effort, not perfection" during the 2026 to 2027 year. Businesses that align with a program starter kit and use it can expect AUSTRAC's engagement to focus on how they apply their program. Sector specific training needs are covered on the pages for [lawyers and accountants](/regulations/aml-ctf-tranche-2-lawyers-accountants-training) and [real estate](/regulations/aml-ctf-tranche-2-real-estate-training).

sections.heading: Which training records does AUSTRAC say demonstrate compliance?

blocks.text: You must keep records reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance with your personnel training obligations, and AUSTRAC's [record keeping overview](https://www.austrac.gov.au/industry-and-business/obligations-and-guidance/your-amlctf-program/develop-your-amlctf-programs/record-keeping/record-keeping-overview) gives examples. AML/CTF program records are generally kept for seven years under section 116.

blocks.caption: Training related records AUSTRAC lists as examples (not exhaustive)
head: Obligation
Records that may demonstrate compliance
rows: Establish ongoing AML/CTF personnel training

Training content and materials reflecting program policies and procedures; training schedules or plans detailing topics, dates, and target staff; register of attendance, results, completion, and action taken in response to non-attendance
Personnel due diligence
Job descriptions, training completion logs or register, qualifications, and internal assessment results, alongside background checks and role change records
Appoint an AML/CTF compliance officer
Role description, appointment records, fit and proper assessment, and evidence of training, skills, and knowledge

Role descriptions, appointment records, and evidence of AML/CTF training, skills, and knowledge
Suspicious matter reporting processes
Training materials and attendance records related to suspicious matter report processes
Review policies when the risk assessment changes
Records of how staff are made aware of relevant policy changes

blocks.text: The training guidance adds detail on what a record could contain: who completed training (names, roles, teams, and start date in the role), what was delivered (topics, format, content, and content version), how understanding was assessed and the results, and training history across initial, refresher, and role specific modules. AUSTRAC also expects records kept in their original format, for example a spreadsheet kept as a spreadsheet rather than converted to PDF.

sections.heading: What should you check before AUSTRAC asks?

blocks.text: Test your training evidence against AUSTRAC's own expectations before AUSTRAC does. This original checklist turns the guidance into checks you can run.

rows: Every role with an AML/CTF function is identified and mapped to training

Register shows completion dates against start dates

No overdue entries, or documented follow-up on each

sections.heading: What is the step by step preparation method?

items: Start from the ML/TF risk assessment and list every function that touches customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, reporting, record keeping, or governance.
Build or refresh the role based training matrix; the [training matrix for a bank](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix-for-a-bank) shows the structure for a financial institution.
Reconcile the register against the current staff list and recent role changes, since AUSTRAC expects training before people take on new duties with different risks.
Pull a sample of five people per high risk role and trace each to the content version, assessment result, and any remediation.
Confirm the compliance officer's reports to the governing body (required at least every 12 months) mention training status and gaps.
Assemble the records in their original formats with an index, and keep them for the retention period. See [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures AML/CTF obligations, program policies, and role risks before training is written, so each module and assessment item traces to the policy and risk it addresses and the register can show who was trained on which version. See [compliance programs](/programs/compliance) and [financial services](/industries/financial-services).

faqs.a: The Rules require ongoing training but do not set a fixed interval. AUSTRAC gives example frequencies, such as every 6 to 12 months for compliance officers and senior management and every 12 months for customer facing staff, and states the frequency must be appropriate to your business and risks.

faqs.q: Can we rely on AUSTRAC's free e-learning?
faqs.a: Not on its own. AUSTRAC says its e-learning modules can be used as part of your training but cannot be relied on solely, because training must be tailored to each person's functions, the risks relevant to those functions, and their responsibilities under your policies.

faqs.q: Do contractors and third party staff need AML/CTF training?
faqs.a: AUSTRAC's guidance uses personnel to mean anyone employed or engaged to perform AML/CTF functions. Its example schedule includes training third party vendors when onboarded and when the contract is renewed or changed. If you outsource delivery of training, you remain responsible for it being tailored and understandable.

faqs.q: How long must AML/CTF training records be kept?
faqs.a: AML/CTF program records, which include training records, are kept under section 116 of the Act; AUSTRAC describes the period as generally seven years, running from the time the record is no longer relevant to demonstrating compliance. Keep superseded training content too, so you can show what a person was trained on.

factCheck.claim: Training guidance: Act s26F(4)(e) and Rules 5-9(2)(3); initial and ongoing training; tailored to functions, risks, responsibilities; easy to understand; expectations list (training plan, updates, steps, register, monitor effectiveness, evaluate retention and application); example frequencies; update triggers including findings from independent evaluations, regulatory or internal compliance reviews; e-learning cannot be relied on solely; outsourcing due diligence; monitoring tools; remedial actions; record keeping s116 with example record details incl content version; third-party vendors at onboarding and renewal. Last updated 27 Mar 2026.

Record keeping overview: records usually kept 7 years; records in original format (Excel as spreadsheet); table: training content and materials, schedules, register of attendance, results, completion and action on non-attendance; PDD records incl training logs; compliance officer and senior manager evidence of training; SMR training materials and attendance; staff awareness of policy changes; governing body reports at least once every 12 months.

Priorities 2026-27: interventions on entities in sectors regulated before 31 March who don't manage risks effectively, including programs not applied in daily operations; 1 July 2026 sectors listed. Last updated 29 Oct 2026.

May 2026 statement (21 May 2026): newly regulated businesses expected to be enrolled, have program and compliance officer, train staff on program, be ready to report; effort not perfection in FY26/27; starter kit users can expect engagement focused on application of program.
